newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Menem tries to heal rifts in party.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Menem tries to heal rifts in party.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem, complaining of "treason" within the ruling party, tried to heal rifts at a weekend retreat and motivate members to overcome a plunge in popularity just months before key polls.

The Peronist leader, speaking to a party national council meeting at a tourist resort, said those working against the mainstream of the party jeopardised the government's continued majority in the lower house of Congress in October elections.

"We cannot accept the duality of treasonous members who wear the Peronist jersey, because they are making fools of us," Menem told cabinet ministers, governors and other Peronist members. "Those who do not want to be in the party, let them leave and I bid them well."

A series of corruption scandals and an unemployment rate of 17.3 percent have contributed to driving down the popularity of Menem's government to below 20 percent from 50 percent when it was reelected in May 1995.
The Peronists, backed by small provincial parties, now control the lower house of Congress with a thin majority.

Rifts in the party have developed in part due to early campaigning for 1999 presidential polls. There have also been deep divisions caused by Peronists in Congress who oppose major administration bills like labour reform.

Rather than engage in debate over policy issues at the national council meeting, as was planned, Menem and his ministers avoided all discussion by giving speeches listing the administration's achievements.
Dissident Peronist Senator Antonio Cafiero complained about the lack of debate and about what he called the government's inability to accept criticism.

"Even though this kind of meeting was opportune, there should have been discussion and it should have been open to suggestions and even criticisms that some aspects of the government's work may have merited."

As a symbol of his efforts to heal divisions, Menem even said he would be willing to accept as a legislative candidate former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, who has accused the government of being infested with corruption since the president fired him in July.

"Cavallo is an excellent economist who wants to enter the world of politics, and if he wants to do it with the Peronists he is welcome to," Menem said. Cavallo, as minister, was not elected and not a member of the Peronist party.

The powerful governor of Buenos Aires, Eduardo Duhalde, whose own wing of the party has been at odds with the Menemists, indicated his intention to seek unity to better fight centrist Radicals and centre-left Frepaso.

"Next year we will meet again, and the first thing we will do is congratulate the president for the electoral victory the Peronists will have this year," said Duhalde, who has declared his intention to run for president in 1999.
